summary:
TerraScope: NISAR Earth Observation Platform
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026  "Dancing with the SARs"
TerraScope is an interactive web app, built for desktop and mobile, that turns NISAR L-band radar data into something people can see and explore: how Earth's surface changes over time. It tracks five types of change in one place: ground deformation, forests and biomass, glaciers, floods and wetlands, and agriculture.
Users start on a 3D globe showing NISAR's orbit (~747 km), swaths and change overlays. They can zoom from orbit down to regional scale and jump to three reference investigations: the Kahramanmaraş M7.8 earthquake rupture, Brahmaputra Basin flooding, and San Joaquin Valley crop growth. A timeline steps through NISAR's 12-day repeat passes with charts of displacement or vegetation index. The Compare Lab adds a before/after swipe curtain with a change overlay plus baseline and coherence checks. Orbit AI explains the radar physics in plain language: what changed, alternative explanations, limitations and how to verify. Provenance details and GeoJSON, CSV, JSON and report exports keep the science transparent and reusable.

TERRA//SCOPE: Project Details

What it does and how it works
TERRA//SCOPE is a web platform that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into an interactive 3D view of how Earth's surface changes. NISAR's synthetic aperture radar (SAR) sends its own microwave pulses and records the echoes. This lets it image land and ice day and night, through cloud, smoke and rain. By comparing the radar signal between repeat passes (InSAR), it can detect ground movement of millimetres to centimetres. NISAR covers nearly all land and ice every 12 days from a 747 km orbit. TERRA//SCOPE lets users explore the surface in 3D, detect where it has changed, compare different dates, and understand what the change means.

Benefits

  • Radar works through cloud and darkness, so observations aren't blocked the way optical imagery is.
  • Raw radar data is hard to read, so the platform presents it in a form non-experts can understand.
  • A regular 12-day revisit supports time-series tracking of slow hazards such as landslides, land subsidence and glacier flow.
  • NISAR data is free and open, so the approach can be reused by anyone.

Intended impact
The goal is to make planetary change visible and easy to act on. This could help researchers, disaster-response teams, city planners, farmers and educators. Examples include spotting unstable slopes or sinking ground early, tracking forest biomass and carbon, monitoring ice and floods, and teaching students how radar satellites observe Earth.

Tools and technology used

  • Data source: NASA-ISRO NISAR mission (L-band and S-band SAR).
  • Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on Netlify. [Add any 3D library you used, such as Three.js or CesiumJS.]
  • Design and presentation: custom dark interface with a cyan and amber colour system.
  • Hardware and software: [Add your development tools and devices.]

How it is creative
Radar data is normally abstract numbers and grey imagery. TERRA//SCOPE treats it as something you can see and explore. It combines three ideas: a 3D "surface-change" view, a four-step flow of explore, detect, compare and understand, and a mission-control look suited to space data. It brings together two agencies' instruments and two radar bands in one place.

Factors considered

  • Accuracy: keep the science faithful to NASA and ISRO mission facts, and label illustrative visuals clearly.
  • Accessibility: keep the language simple and the interface readable for non-specialists.
  • Performance: keep 3D views responsive on ordinary devices.
  • Openness: use free and open data so others can verify and build on the work.
  • Responsible use: show uncertainty honestly and avoid overstating what radar can detect.
